name: Languages (Accept-Language and navigator.languages)
plain: Ordered list of the person's preferred languages, sent on every request.
meaning: Shows native language, second languages and country (en-US vs en-GB, es-419). A multilingual list narrows identity sharply: 5.9 bits in 2016. Sites localize with it; trackers fingerprint it.

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

limits.headline: Can see the languages you prefer, in order, with every page request
limits.user_action: Nothing. Your browser sends it every time a page loads
can: See your first language and backups, such as en-US then es
Show the page in your language
Guess your country from the language variant, such as en-GB or es-419
Add to a profile that helps recognise your browser
cannot: Know your exact location from it
See languages you have not set in your browser
Be turned off on its own; you change it in browser settings

story.what_it_is: Every request tells the site your preferred languages, in order.

marketing.name: Accept-Language
marketing.pitch: Describes the header where browsers list the languages a person prefers so servers can reply in the right one.

story.for_you: You open a site and it appears in your language, or offers a banner to switch. You never see the list of languages your browser sent. If you speak several, that list may be the most telling part.
story.for_makers: Sites use it to pick the language and currency. Ad, fraud and tracking systems also use the exact list as a clue about who you are, since few people share the same mix of languages.

use_cases.example: A game site shows the lobby and rules in your language and puts you in a regional server list.
A cloud gaming site picks the store language and subtitles without asking.
A store shows prices and sizes in your region's format.
A streaming site picks audio and subtitle defaults from your language list.
An ad network targets by language and region, using the list as a profile clue.
A fraud check compares languages with the IP country, since a mismatch may mean a stolen account.
A fingerprinting script mixes the language list with other clues to spot a repeat visitor.

technical_bounds: Browser UI language is not always system language

linkedin.how: Collected as language. Read by the LinkedIn APFC fingerprint script (alleged by BrowserGate, partly confirmed by BleepingComputer).
